passages.quote:
I Knew’ is a month-long public health campaign developed by Chapter One to address gambling harms among men aged 18 to 35. The campaign aims to increase understanding of modern-day gambling, reduce stigma, and encourage men to seek support earlier.

The campaign focused on how gambling products are designed to encourage continued play, the realities of the gambling industry business model and the benefits of life without gambling, using relatable stories and local imagery. These stories explore the impact that gambling can have on mental health and relationships, while emphasising that it is never too late to make a positive change.

By increasing awareness of gambling-related harms and encouraging earlier help-seeking, the campaign aims to support men to better understand the risks associated with gambling and access support when needed. The approach aligns with the Men’s Health Strategy’s focus on addressing gambling harms among young men and promoting early intervention.

Developing healthy living and working conditions

Where people live, work and learn has a significant influence on their health outcomes. Local systems can improve men’s health by creating environments that support healthy behaviours, reduce health risks and make it easier for men to access support. This includes using workplaces, educational settings and community spaces as opportunities to connect men with health services and prevention activity.

Practical examples include:

working with both large and small local employers to support positive health behaviours. This could include working with traditionally male-dominated sectors as well as larger employers with substantial male workforces to:

promote employees’ access to occupational health services

promote flexible working arrangements that support attendance at health appointments and reflect men’s parenting and caring responsibilities

use the workplace or working environment as a setting to deliver outreach services to male employees

promote employee codes of practice and toolkits such as the British Standard on suicide prevention, Construction Leadership Council mental health joint code of practice (PDF, 18.2 MB) and BITC/Public Health England toolkits

promote use of existing digital behaviour change tools and apps such as the NHS Healthy Choices Quiz, NHS Active 10 app, NHS Quit Smoking app and Mind Plan

local authorities and NHS organisations leading by example through workplace policies and cultures that support health, wellbeing and prevention

supporting parents, carers, educators and other trusted adults to help boys and young men navigate online environments safely, including by promoting resources such as:

the Kids Online Safety Hub which contains content on misogyny and supporting conversations about harmful online narratives

Educate Against Hate to safeguard students against radicalisation

the updated relationships, sex and health education (RSHE) guidance covering online harms, misinformation, social media, artificial intelligence and deepfakes

tackling structural contributors to poor health outcomes and inequalities that contribute to men’s health outcomes, for example, influencing planning and environmental design to tackle the impact of a lack of access to green space and quality housing, as well as the impacts of air pollution

Case study: workplace health checks for routine and manual workers in Essex

Essex County Council’s SISU mobile digital health checks programme brings preventative healthcare directly into workplace settings, improving access for routine and manual workers who may face barriers to engaging with traditional health services.

The programme has:

delivered over 6,500 health checks across 94 Essex employers

encouraged eligible users to contact their GP for a full NHS Health Check

prompted 2,000 referrals to local services for smoking cessation, weight management, blood pressure and mental health support

Digital health check stations allow employees to complete a health check in just 4 to 6 minutes, with 24-hour access available to accommodate shift work and non-standard working patterns. 23.2% of checks were completed outside GP hours, demonstrating improved access to preventative services for people who may face work-related barriers.

Employee data reported that following checks:

95% of users made healthier lifestyle changes

91.4% acted on flagged issues

94% accessed follow-on support

Although not aimed at men specifically, the programme seeks to address issues that can disproportionately affect men including access to health services, health behaviours and health literacy. The programme’s 55% male engagement suggests that opportunistic health checks delivered outside primary care settings are an effective way of reaching men.

By embedding preventative health support within workplaces and making it easier to access around working lives, the programme demonstrates how employers can play a role in supporting healthier living and improving access to early prevention.

Fostering strong social, family and community networks

Social, community and family networks are a critical determinant of health outcomes. Local partners can play an important role in creating opportunities for men and boys to build and maintain meaningful connections. Fatherhood is an important life stage that can significantly affect men’s health and wellbeing, with the transition to parenthood presenting both challenges and opportunities to engage men in improving their health.

Practical examples include:

identifying, connecting with and amplifying local community organisations that support men’s health, including by promoting their services through local networks and strengthening referral routes into them

Regularly considering sex differences within local data, alongside disability, ethnicity, sexual orientation, age and deprivation, can help areas identify where there is the greatest unmet need and target action more effectively.

Platforms such as Fingertips and Spotlight bring together hundreds of indicators on population health, health inequalities, risk factors, behaviours, service uptake and outcomes, allowing users to compare local areas with regional and national benchmarks, where available. The LG Inform men’s health report (published 2026) provides a valuable source of local intelligence, enabling local authorities to explore and compare progress against a range of indicators and identify opportunities to target support where needed. Local data sources such as healthcare or locally commissioned service data may also provide more timely information that can be used for local needs assessments.

Local partners can consider where gaps in data limit understanding of men’s health outcomes, experiences or service use, and whether existing data collection and reporting arrangements could be used or adapted to support more effective planning, commissioning and service delivery. For example, where appropriate and proportionate, considering sex-disaggregated reporting on outcomes within contracts can provide understanding of what is working.

Partners can also work with community organisations run for men to help organisations build the evidence base for their contribution to health and wellbeing outcomes.

Further examples of how local systems can use data and insight are included throughout this guidance.

Governance and accountability

Local system leaders have a crucial role in driving progress on men’s health. By providing clear governance, senior ownership and accountability, they can help embed men’s health within existing priorities. This section provides examples of how men’s health can be built into governance, planning and performance arrangements.

ICBs and NHS providers

NHS organisations have statutory duties to reduce health inequalities, including duties relating to gender and sex. Health inequalities are defined as avoidable differences in health outcomes between groups or populations - such as differences in how long we live, or the age at which we get preventable diseases or health conditions.

In line with the Core20PLUS5 approach, NHS organisations are encouraged to draw on data and intelligence from a range of sources to build a robust understanding of men’s health and wellbeing needs across the life course, including how these vary between population groups and places. This can build on existing integrated needs assessments, joint strategic needs assessments (JSNAs) and neighbourhood health plans.

At a minimum, performance, quality and outcomes data can be disaggregated by sex, age, ethnicity and deprivation, and embedded in routine reporting to identify inequalities in access, experience and outcomes, including across relevant indicators within the NHS Oversight Framework.

Quantitative data could be combined with qualitative and community insight data to understand the barriers that may prevent men from accessing or engaging with care, including digital exclusion, transport barriers and the accessibility and flexibility of services.

These insights can help to establish a clear starting point and inform strategic commissioning decisions and measurable improvement plans, with progress tracked against relevant outcome goals to determine whether healthcare inequalities are reducing.

Combined strategic authorities

Combined strategic authorities can use their strengthened health duties to address the structural drivers of men’s health inequalities, while ensuring alignment with related agendas, such as jobs and skills growth and healthy workplaces. Operating across a wider geography can help authorities bring together data and insight on groups of men whose needs may be harder to understand or respond to within a single local authority. Their role can include:

convening partners

aligning action on employment, skills, transport and housing with local health priorities

supporting delivery through existing local services

Local authorities

As the local authority’s statutory source of public health expertise, directors of public health can play an important role in informing local priorities and supporting evidence-based action. Directors of public health can use reports including the JSNA, specific in depth needs assessments, and their annual directors of public health reports to raise awareness of men’s health issues, highlight local inequalities and stimulate action across the wider system. Local authorities are encouraged to ensure that recommendations from these reports are implemented and monitored through the HWB.

Elected members can play an important role in scrutinising local system progress from neighbourhoods to across the authority and its partners. The Local Government Association’s Must know: supporting men’s health guidance supports councillors to encourage officers and partners to understand local needs.

The health scrutiny committee also provides a more formal opportunity to investigate how well system partners are addressing men’s health inequalities and review performance.

Health and wellbeing boards (HWBs)

The convening role of HWBs can also be a useful vehicle for accountability on men’s health. HWBs can look at how men’s health is considered in the JSNA and in the subsequent strategies developed by partners, including neighbourhood delivery plans. Part of this could also consider the involvement and engagement of local men as well as analysis of sex and gender differences when designing commissioning and delivery models of services.

HWBs may also consider whether a local men’s health or gender equality plan could be needed to accelerate and co-ordinate action.

ntion within mental health support, including mental health neighbourhood centres, with a concentration on sex and gender and intersectionality, to ensure pathways meet the needs of those at highest risk of suicide, self-harm and poor mental health

promoting staying safe from suicide guidance by ensuring that all mental health practitioners across all providers undertake training and deliver care in line with the guidance

ensuring men at risk of suicide can access urgent, tailored support, with signposting and referral available through different services with specific consideration of the needs of higher risk groups such as gay and bisexual men, disabled men and some specific ethnic groups

using a variety of trusted, non-clinical routes to raise awareness of and provide mental health and wellbeing support

ensuring mental health services use language and approaches that resonate with target groups of men, avoid stereotypes about help-seeking, and provide a timely and credible response when men do seek support. For example, considering how men describe distress, the quality of first contact, continuity and follow-up, and whether service models fit with the practical realities of men’s lives

continuously monitoring the outcomes of initiatives that are operating in local areas for evidence of greater health literacy, subsequent access to health services where needed and recovery. For example, the Men’s Health Community Fund will include an evaluation of the programme to strengthen the evidence base on community-based approaches to improving men’s health and wellbeing, with findings published to support future policy and practice

using population health management tools and local insight to proactively identify men who may be at risk of developing health conditions, such as undiagnosed respiratory disease, or poor mental health and suicide, recognising that men may be less likely to engage with traditional healthcare services

ensuring implementation of the cardiovascular disease modern service framework (MSF) and other MSFs align with the principles for equitable implementation

delivering NHS Health Checks in non-clinical, trusted settings that men use, such as workplaces, to encourage uptake, particularly among groups of men most at risk, as part of a broader approach to reducing inequalities

promoting awareness of signs and symptoms of major conditions among men, such as cancer, cardiovascular disease and respiratory disease, ensuring messaging is tailored to target audiences

promoting awareness and uptake among men of screening programmes such as for lung and bowel cancer

developing and implementing local HIV action plans that align with national objectives and reflect local population needs, considering the 5 populations disproportionately affected by HIV, as set out in the government’s HIV Action Plan. This includes the following groups of men, among others:

ethnic minority gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM)

White GBMSM

Black African heterosexual men

considering the needs of male service users within fertility services and providing services that are responsive to their needs. NICE guidance outlines how male fertility problems can be investigated

Case study: harnessing the power of football to support suicide prevention

The North London NHS Foundation Trust has worked in partnership with Arsenal in the community for 15 years, running a mental health football programme. This relationship led to further collaboration on the Premier League funded Together Against Suicide project, and the provision of a specialist mental health nurse working with the club. This is the second season of the Together Against Suicide initiative.

A nurse is on-site before, during and after all Premier League home matches, operating a confidential drop-in service. Each person accessing the service is provided with a specialist clinical assessment, intervention and signposting to community services for follow up.

Having a specialist nurse as part of the project has ensured clinical decisions have been made with confidence, using robust risk assessments and other NHS resources to inform the work. The NHS and Arsenal partnership aims to destigmatise those seeking access to mental health care and reach people in non-clinical settings.

Conclusion

This guidance is intended to help system partners turn the ambitions of the Men’s Health Strategy into local action. Once the foundations for action are in place, local partners can build on them in ways that reflect local needs, priorities and opportunities, embedding consideration of men’s health more systematically across services, policies and wider system planning. Over time, systems can build on what works and share their learning with others.

Further guidance and resources developed by the men’s health sector that can support local implementation can be found on our men’s health resource hub.

We will keep this guidance under review as practice develops. To provide feedback on this guidance or to share suggestions of good practice, contact us at menshealth@dhsc.gov.uk.

Acknowledgements

This guidance has been developed through extensive engagement with partners across health, local government, academia, the voluntary and community sector, and professional bodies.

We would like to express our sincere thanks to Professor Paul Galdas, the Association of Directors of Public Health (ADPH) and the Local Government Association (LGA) for their close collaboration in developing this guidance. We are also grateful to the Men’s Health Stakeholder Group and the Men’s Health Academic Network who shared evidence, expertise and practical examples throughout its development. Their insights have helped to shape a guidance document that reflects the realities of local delivery and highlights opportunities to improve the health and wellbeing of men and boys across England.
